As regards liability, insurance company has raised statutory defence that the offending vehicle was being driven by respondent no.1 in breach of the condition of the insurance policy.
It has been specifically pleaded that the driver of the offending vehicle did not have a valid driving licence.
To prove the same, insurance company examined Daksh Arora as R3W1.
R3W1 duly proved service of notice u/O 12 Rule 8 CPC upon the driver and the owner.
Despite such service, driver and owner did not produce any driving licence and did not even cross examine R3W1.
Hence, it stands proved that the driver of the offending vehicle was driving without a valid driving licence which is a breach of conditions of insurance policy.
Secondly, the petitioners have also proved by relying on the DAR and the chargesheet that the offending driver was under the influence of alcohol beyond the permissible limit.
Driving while drunk is further a breach of the terms of insurance policy.
Owner of the offending vehicle has not taken any defence that he had not authorized the driver/respondent no.1 to drive his vehicle.
As such, driver and owner of such offending vehicle are primarily jointly and severally liable to compensate the petitioners.

sentences.text: Even otherwise there is nothing in newly inserted Section 150 MV Act which bars the Tribunal from directing the insurance company to pay compensation to the third party and later recover the compensation from the owner and driver in cases where a breach of policy has been committed.

There is nothing in the said provision which can be read as complete exoneration of the liability of the insurance company from paying the compensation where the existence of the policy is not disputed.

Accordingly, as it is not disputed that the offending vehicle was duly insured, the liability to compensate the victims would fall upon the insurance company, which would be at liberty to recover Harish Salikram (Dar) vs Vinay (291/23Gk) on 16 December, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/36598268/

the provision of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 ("the Act", for short) makes it clear that the award must be just, which means that compensation should, to the extent possible, fully and adequately restore the claimant to the position prior to the accident.
The object of awarding damages is to make good the loss suffered as a result of wrong done as far as money can do so, in a fair, reasonable and equitable manner.

The court or the Tribunal shall have to assess the damages objectively and exclude from consideration any speculation or fancy, though some conjecture with reference to the nature of disability and its consequences, is inevitable.
A person is not only to be compensated for the physical injury, but also for the loss which he suffered as a result of such injury.

This means that he is to be compensated for his inability to lead a full life, his inability to enjoy those normal amenities which he would have enjoyed but for the injuries, and his inability to earn as much as he used to earn or could have earned.
